claim: When exercise starts, oxygen uptake (VO2) in muscle and at the lungs rises in a near-exponential curve toward the 'steady-state' demand, and it can take 2-4 min, or even longer at higher work rates, to get there. Slow VO2 kinetics increase the 'O2 deficit', which has to be met by anaerobic ATP sources: breakdown of muscle high-energy phosphates and lactate made from glycogen. At higher intensities VO2 keeps creeping up even at a constant work rate (the 'slow component').
plain: For the first 2-4 minutes your oxygen supply hasn't caught up with the work, so your muscles borrow quick energy that doesn't need oxygen (stored phosphates, and sugar turned into lactate).
source: Jones AM, Poole DC (2005). Oxygen uptake dynamics: from muscle to mouth - an introduction to the symposium. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise 37(9):1542-1550.
exact_words: However, it can take 2-4 min, or even longer at higher work rates, before this steady state is attained.
who: Introduction to a symposium on VO2 kinetics: it summarizes earlier exercise research and does not report a new study
limits: Describes a single step up to steady exercise. It does not measure how hard the start feels. Ashtanga's changing postures and breath-paced vinyasas were not studied.

claim: In competitive soccer players, quadriceps muscle temperature rose from 36.0 °C at rest to 39.4 °C after the pre-game warm-up and stayed there through the first half. It fell to 37.4 °C during a passive half-time, and sprint performance at the start of the second half dropped 2.4%. Players who did low-intensity re-warm-up at half-time kept muscle temperature up and had no drop in sprint performance. The fall in muscle temperature correlated with the fall in performance (r = 0.60).
plain: In soccer players, warming up raised thigh-muscle temperature by about 3 °C. Resting through half-time cooled the muscle and sprints were 2.4% slower, while players who kept moving lightly kept their sprint speed.
source: Mohr M, Krustrup P, Nybo L, Nielsen JJ, Bangsbo J (2004). Muscle temperature and sprint performance during soccer matches - beneficial effect of re-warm-up at half-time. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports 14(3):156-162.
exact_words: T(m) was 36.0+/-0.2 degrees C at rest and increased (P<0.05) to 39.4+/-0.2 degrees C before the game and remained unaltered during the first half.
who: Competitive soccer players, n=25 (temperature tracked in 9; half-time re-warm-up 8 vs passive rest 8)
limits: Measures sprint power in soccer, not endurance, flexibility or yoga. Small groups. The study does not say how many minutes of warm-up it took to reach 39.4 °C.

claim: The classic 'second wind' (a period of marked exercise intolerance and racing heart rate that clears after about 6-10 min, then exercise feels easier) is described as an almost unique feature of McArdle disease, in which muscles cannot break down their own glycogen. The authors explain that it arrives once more blood-borne fuel (especially glucose, plus fatty acids) reaches the working muscle. Higher aerobic fitness and an active lifestyle were associated with a higher workload at which the second wind appeared.
plain: A sharp 'now it gets easier' moment after 6-10 minutes is almost unique to people with a rare muscle disease (McArdle disease), whose muscles can't use their stored sugar. It comes as sugar and fat from the blood reach the muscle.
source: Salazar-Martínez E, Santalla A, Valenzuela PL, et al., Lucia A (2021). The Second Wind in McArdle Patients: Fitness Matters. Frontiers in Physiology 12:744632.
exact_words: disappearance of previous tachycardia (i.e., the actual "SW") until 6-10 min has elapsed-is an almost unique feature of McArdle disease
who: McArdle disease patients, n=54 (24 women), mean age 33
limits: These are patients with a muscle enzyme defect, and the study is cross-sectional (association, not cause). A sharp, measurable second wind in healthy people is not well documented; their hard start is better explained by the oxygen deficit (energy-01).

claim: Cardiovascular drift is a slow, progressive fall in stroke volume, with a matching rise in heart rate, that begins after 10-20 min of steady prolonged exercise. The authors propose it is driven mainly by the rising heart rate (less time for the heart to fill), not mainly by more blood going to the skin as body temperature rises.
plain: After 10-20 minutes at the same effort your heart starts beating a bit faster and pumping a bit less each beat, even though you aren't working harder.
source: Coyle EF, González-Alonso J (2001). Cardiovascular drift during prolonged exercise: new perspectives. Exercise and Sport Sciences Reviews 29(2):88-92.
exact_words: We propose that cardiovascular drift, characterized by a progressive decline in stroke volume after 10-20 min of exercise, is primarily due to increased heart rate
who: Review of studies in humans doing prolonged steady exercise (mostly trained cyclists)
limits: The drift itself is well established, but the cause is the authors' proposal and is still debated. Not measured in yoga.

claim: Using stable isotope tracers and indirect calorimetry, the study found that during 2 h of exercise at 65% VO2max, oxidation of fuels from the blood (plasma glucose and plasma fatty acids) rose steadily over time, while oxidation of the muscle's own stores (muscle glycogen and muscle triglyceride) fell. Fat breakdown in fat tissue (peripheral lipolysis) peaked at the lowest intensity (25% VO2max); muscle glycogen use rose with intensity.
plain: In 2 hours of steady exercise, trained people's muscles used less of their own stored sugar and fat as time went on, and took more fuel (sugar and fat) from the blood.
source: Romijn JA, Coyle EF, Sidossis LS, Gastaldelli A, Horowitz JF, Endert E, Wolfe RR (1993). Regulation of endogenous fat and carbohydrate metabolism in relation to exercise intensity and duration. American Journal of Physiology 265(3 Pt 1):E380-E391.
exact_words: During 2 h of exercise at 65% VO2max plasma-derived substrate oxidation progressively increased over time, whereas muscle glycogen and triglyceride oxidation decreased.
who: Endurance-trained subjects, n=5, at 25, 65 and 85% VO2max
limits: Only 5 trained people in a lab. It shows a fuel shift over time, not that it causes fat loss or better health.

claim: During 4 h of light exercise (about 30% VO2max), blood glucose stayed flat for the first 40 min, then fell progressively to 30% below baseline. Beyond 40 min, the share of the legs' oxygen use coming from free fatty acids rose steadily to 62%, while glucose's share fell from 40% to 30% between 90 and 240 min. Total glucose output from the splanchnic (liver and gut) region over 4 h (75 g) was estimated as enough to use up about 75% of liver glycogen stores.
plain: In 4 hours of easy exercise, after about 40 minutes the leg muscles drew more and more of their energy from fat carried in the blood, reaching about 60% by the end.
source: Ahlborg G, Felig P, Hagenfeldt L, Hendler R, Wahren J (1974). Substrate turnover during prolonged exercise in man: splanchnic and leg metabolism of glucose, free fatty acids, and amino acids. Journal of Clinical Investigation 53(4):1080-1090.
exact_words: As exercise was continued beyond 40 min, the relative contribution of FFA to total oxygen metabolism rose progressively to 62%.
who: Healthy subjects, n=6, 4 h at about 30% of maximal oxygen uptake
limits: Small 1970s study at a light, steady workload; it measures leg metabolism only, not whole-body fat loss. The 62% was reached only after about 4 hours.

claim: The 'crossover' concept: the fuel mix at any moment depends on intensity (which pushes muscle toward carbohydrate through glycogen breakdown, a changed pattern of muscle-fibre recruitment and more sympathetic nervous system drive) versus endurance training (which pushes toward fat burning). The literature it reviews indicates that after training, low-intensity exercise (≤45% VO2max) runs mainly on fat, while hard exercise (about 75% VO2max) runs mainly on carbohydrate. The crossover point is the power output above which carbohydrate predominates.
plain: In trained people, easy exercise runs mainly on fat and hard exercise runs mainly on sugar. Endurance training tips the balance toward fat at any given effort.
source: Brooks GA, Mercier J (1994). Balance of carbohydrate and lipid utilization during exercise: the "crossover" concept. Journal of Applied Physiology 76(6):2253-2261.
exact_words: after endurance training, exercise at low intensities (< or = 45% maximal O2 uptake) is accomplished with lipid as the main substrate.
who: Theoretical framework built from published human exercise studies
limits: A model about intensity and training, not duration. It does not measure any yoga practice.

claim: Seven endurance-trained cyclists rode at 71% VO2max to fatigue. With a placebo drink, fatigue came after about 3.0 h and was preceded by a fall in blood glucose to 2.5 mM and a fall in RER (a shift away from carbohydrate). Thigh muscle glycogen was used fastest in the first 2 h (51.5 mmol/kg/h) and more slowly in the third hour (23.0). Drinking carbohydrate kept blood glucose up and extended exercise by about 1 h (to 4.0 h), without changing muscle glycogen use over the first 3 h.
plain: In hard, long cycling, muscles burned their stored sugar fastest in the first 2 hours. On flavoured water alone the riders gave out at about 3 hours, after their blood sugar fell; with a sugar drink they kept going about 1 hour longer.
source: Coyle EF, Coggan AR, Hemmert MK, Ivy JL (1986). Muscle glycogen utilization during prolonged strenuous exercise when fed carbohydrate. Journal of Applied Physiology 61(1):165-172.
exact_words: Fatigue during the placebo trial occurred after 3.02 +/- 0.19 h of exercise and was preceded by a decline (P less than 0.01) in plasma glucose to 2.5 +/- 0.5 mM
who: Endurance-trained cyclists, n=7, at 71% VO2max
limits: Hard continuous cycling far above typical yoga intensity; it does not show that a 90-120 min Mysore practice empties glycogen.

claim: More than two in five marathon runners report 'hitting the wall', the rapid onset of severe fatigue caused by near-complete depletion of carbohydrate in leg muscles and liver. A computational model estimates that the distance to the wall depends on running intensity (% VO2max), leg muscle mass, and muscle and liver glycogen density. For runners at 80-95% VO2max the modelled failure point clusters around mile 21 (km 33-34), where surveys find the wall most often. The model predicts few runners would hit it before mile 11, or when running below about 55% VO2max.
plain: Runners who 'hit the wall' have nearly run out of stored sugar. It happens most often around kilometre 33, and a computer model suggests few would hit it at an easy pace.
source: Rapoport BI (2010). Metabolic factors limiting performance in marathon runners. PLoS Computational Biology 6(10):e1000960.
exact_words: more than two in five report ‘hitting the wall,’ the rapid onset of severe fatigue and inability to maintain a high-intensity pace, resulting from the near-complete depletion of carbohydrate stores in the leg muscles and liver.
who: No participants: a computational model based on published physiology of marathon runners, plus earlier survey data (Buman et al.)
limits: The distances are model estimates, not measurements, and assume continuous running; they do not apply to lower-intensity yoga.

claim: Eight trained cyclists rode 2 h at 62-67% VO2max in warm conditions (33 °C, 50% humidity) while drinking enough to replace 0%, 20%, 48% or 81% of sweat loss, ending 4.2%, 3.4%, 2.3% or 1.1% lighter. The more dehydrated they became, the more core temperature and heart rate rose and stroke volume fell, in a near-straight-line relationship (r = 0.98-0.99). The largest fluid intake reduced overheating, apparently through higher skin blood flow.
plain: The more water you sweat out and don't drink back, the hotter you get and the harder your heart has to work at the same effort.
source: Montain SJ, Coyle EF (1992). Influence of graded dehydration on hyperthermia and cardiovascular drift during exercise. Journal of Applied Physiology 73(4):1340-1350.
exact_words: the magnitude of increase in core temperature and HR and the decline in SV are graded in proportion to the amount of dehydration accrued during exercise.
who: Endurance-trained cyclists, n=8, age about 23, 2 h at 62-67% VO2max in 33 °C
limits: Lab cycling with fan wind; it does not give a fluid plan for yoga, and Mysore practice does not usually allow drinking mid-session.

claim: Trained cyclists exercising at 60% VO2max in 40 °C heat all stopped at the same internal temperature (esophageal about 40.1-40.2 °C, muscle about 40.7-40.9 °C), with heart rate at 196-198 beats/min, whatever temperature they started at. Starting hotter shortened time to exhaustion (63, 46 and 28 min when starting at about 36, 37 and 38 °C). Heart rate rose and stroke volume fell in parallel with rising core temperature.
plain: In strong heat the body stops you when your inside gets to about 40 °C, so starting cooler gives you more time.
source: González-Alonso J, Teller C, Andersen SL, Jensen FB, Hyldig T, Nielsen B (1999). Influence of body temperature on the development of fatigue during prolonged exercise in the heat. Journal of Applied Physiology 86(3):1032-1039.
exact_words: These results demonstrate that high internal body temperature per se causes fatigue in trained subjects during prolonged exercise in uncompensable hot environments.
who: Trained cyclists, n=7 for the three starting-temperature trials; 4 cyclists did two extra bouts testing the rate of heat storage. All rode at 60% VO2max in 40 °C.
limits: Extreme lab heat (40 °C) where the body could not shed heat; a normal Bangkok shala is milder and yoga is lower intensity.

claim: In 60-min sessions measured by indirect calorimetry, vinyasa yoga averaged 3.6 METs, against 4.4 METs for self-paced brisk walking and 4.7 METs for walking matched to the yoga heart rate. The authors conclude vinyasa yoga meets the criteria for moderate-intensity physical activity. Because walking at the same heart rate burned more energy, this suggests heart rate overstates the energy cost of yoga.
plain: A 60-minute flowing yoga class counts as moderate exercise, a little easier than a brisk walk, and your heart rate makes it look harder than the calories show.
source: Sherman SA, Rogers RJ, Davis KK, Minster RL, Creasy SA, Mullarkey NC, O'Dell M, Donahue P, Jakicic JM (2017). Energy Expenditure in Vinyasa Yoga Versus Walking. Journal of Physical Activity and Health 14(8):597-605.
exact_words: YOGA meets the criteria for moderate-intensity physical activity.
who: Adults, n=38 (20 men, 18 women), 60-min vinyasa yoga versus treadmill walking
limits: A 60-min vinyasa class, not a 90-120 min traditional Ashtanga Mysore practice. At this intensity the marathon 'wall' (energy-08, energy-09) is unlikely to apply.

claim: Transient hypofrontality hypothesis: the brain is competitive and has finite metabolic resources, so during exercise the heavy neural activation needed to run motor patterns, take in sensory input and coordinate autonomic regulation is proposed to cause a transient decrease of activity in brain structures not needed for the exercise, such as the prefrontal cortex. The author offers this as an account of exercise's effects on emotion and cognition, proposed 'primarily on the strength of its heuristic value'.
plain: The idea is that while the body exercises, the brain's 'thinking boss' at the front gets less energy and goes quieter.
source: Dietrich A, 2006, 'Transient hypofrontality as a mechanism for the psychological effects of exercise', Psychiatry Research 145:79-83
exact_words: during exercise the extensive neural activation required to run motor patterns, assimilate sensory inputs, and coordinate autonomic regulation results in a concomitant transient decrease of neural activity in brain structures, such as the prefrontal cortex, that are not pertinent to performing the exercise
who: None (theory paper with no new data; builds on Dietrich 2003, Consciousness and Cognition 12:231-256, which applies the same idea to endurance running, meditation and other altered states)
limits: This is a proposal, not a measurement. It does not show that prefrontal activity actually drops during exercise (see BRAIN-3 and BRAIN-4).

claim: In two experiments built to test the hypofrontality idea, athletes exercising at a sustained, moderate pace did worse than sedentary controls on a neuropsychological test that depends heavily on the prefrontal cortex. On a test that relies little on the prefrontal cortex, their scores were unaffected.
plain: While exercising steadily at a moderate pace, athletes scored worse than non-exercisers on a thinking test that leans on the front of the brain, but not on a test that doesn't.
when: during sustained moderate exercise (exact duration not given in the abstract)
source: Dietrich A, Sparling PB, 2004, 'Endurance exercise selectively impairs prefrontal-dependent cognition', Brain and Cognition 55:516-524
exact_words: Results showed that during exercise performance on tests demanding prefrontal-dependent cognition was impaired, while at the same time, cognitive processes requiring little prefrontal activity were unaffected.
who: Athletes exercising at a moderate pace compared with sedentary controls, two experiments (sample sizes not stated in the abstract)
limits: A small early test that compared different people (exercising athletes vs sedentary controls) and measured test scores, not brain activity.

claim: In 11 ultramarathon runners tested before, during and after a 6-hour run, frontal-cortex EEG beta activity decreased, with no change in global beta or in frontal or global alpha. Cognitive performance and event-related potentials stayed stable for all 6 hours. Self-rated flow and physical relaxation rose significantly after 1 hour, then fell over the next 5 hours. The authors conclude that the drop in frontal activity supports transient hypofrontality but did not impair cognition, and that cortical activity and flow 'may not be linked as previously supposed'.
plain: During a 6-hour run, the front of the brain got quieter but runners could still think as well as before. The 'in the zone' feeling rose in the first hour, then faded over the next 5 hours.
when: 60+ min (peak flow at 1 h of a 6-h run)
source: Wollseiffen P, Schneider S, Martin LA, Kerhervé HA, Klein T, Solomon C, 2016, 'The effect of 6 h of running on brain activity, mood, and cognitive performance', Experimental Brain Research 234:1829-1836
exact_words: Perceived physical relaxation and flow state increased significantly after 1 h of running but decreased during the following 5 h.
who: Ultramarathon runners, n=11 (6 female, 5 male)
limits: Only 11 runners and no control group. EEG beta is a rough index of activity. The quieter frontal cortex did not reduce thinking ability and did not track the flow feeling.

claim: A systematic review and meta-regression of 21 near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS) studies (291 healthy people) found that incremental exercise brings moderate-to-large increases in prefrontal oxygenation and blood volume. Oxygenation rises from moderate to hard intensity, peaks at hard intensity and drops only at very hard intensities (at or above VO2peak), a quadratic response. Trained people kept higher cortical oxygen levels at very hard intensities than untrained people.
plain: Light-sensor scans show the front of the brain gets more oxygen as exercise goes from moderate to hard; it drops only when you go all-out.
source: Rooks CR, Thom NJ, McCully KK, Dishman RK, 2010, 'Effects of incremental exercise on cerebral oxygenation measured by near-infrared spectroscopy: a systematic review', Progress in Neurobiology 92:134-150
exact_words: prefrontal oxygenation measured with NIRS in healthy people showed a quadratic response to incremental exercise, rising between moderate and hard intensities, then falling at very hard intensities.
who: 291 healthy people in 21 studies (plus 222 heart or lung patients in 6 studies)
limits: The studies used short ramp tests, not hour-long steady sessions, and oxygenation reflects blood supply rather than neural activity directly. It gives no sign that the prefrontal cortex is short of oxygen at moderate pace, but it cannot rule out lower neural activity there.

claim: A meta-regression of acute-exercise studies found that cognitive task performance was impaired during exercise (mean effect -0.14), but only in the first 20 minutes. After that, exercise arousal enhanced performance on tasks involving rapid decisions and automatized behaviors. After exercise, performance improved (mean effect 0.20). Treadmill running impaired performance during exercise, while cycling enhanced it.
plain: For the first 20 minutes the brain is a bit clumsy at tasks; after that, quick, automatic tasks get better.
when: start 0-10 min and 10-30 min (impairment limited to the first 20 min), plus after
source: Lambourne K, Tomporowski P, 2010, 'The effect of exercise-induced arousal on cognitive task performance: a meta-regression analysis', Brain Research 1341:12-24
exact_words: However, impairments were only observed during the first 20min of exercise.
who: Pooled published acute-exercise studies (the abstract does not state the number of studies or participants)
limits: The effects are small and come from lab cognitive tasks, not yoga. Running still impaired performance during exercise. Brain activity was not measured.

claim: A review of flow neuroscience proposes that an attentional account is the best way to advance flow theory, and that it may help explain how an objectively difficult task can feel subjectively effortless. It calls the neuroimaging evidence for prominent hypofrontality accounts 'equivocal', but reports clear indications of reduced activity in brain regions linked to self-referential processing.
plain: In 'the zone', brain areas that think about 'me' seem to quiet down; the idea that the thinking front of the brain powers down has mixed evidence.
source: Harris DJ, Vine SJ, Wilson MR, 2017, 'Neurocognitive mechanisms of the flow state', Progress in Brain Research 234:221-243
exact_words: findings already provide important insights into the crucial role played by higher-order attentional networks, and clear indications of reduced activity in brain regions linked to self-referential processing.
who: Narrative review of brain-imaging studies of flow in sport and lab tasks
limits: A narrative review of few, small studies that are not specific to long exercise. The authors call the neuroscience of flow 'preliminary'.

claim: PET scans with an opioid ligand in 10 athletes, at rest and after 2 hours of endurance running (21.5 ± 4.7 km), showed reduced opioid receptor availability after running, mainly in prefrontal and limbic/paralimbic regions. Euphoria rose significantly after running and correlated inversely with opioid binding in the prefrontal/orbitofrontal cortex, anterior cingulate, insula and temporoparietal regions. The authors read this as support for the 'opioid theory' of the runner's high.
plain: After a 2-hour run, brain scans showed signs that the body's own opioids had been released in mood areas, and the runners who felt most euphoric showed the strongest signs.
source: Boecker H, Sprenger T, Spilker ME, Henriksen G, Koppenhoefer M, Wagner KJ, Valet M, Berthele A, Tolle TR, 2008, 'The runner's high: opioidergic mechanisms in the human brain', Cerebral Cortex 18:2523-2531
exact_words: The level of euphoria was significantly increased after running and was inversely correlated with opioid binding in prefrontal/orbitofrontal cortices, the anterior cingulate cortex, bilateral insula, parainsular cortex, and temporoparietal regions.
who: Male endurance athletes, n=10 (each scanned at rest and after running)
limits: With n=10, only correlation and no opioid blocker, it does not show that opioids cause the high. Opioid release is inferred from lower binding of a non-selective tracer, not measured directly. A later PET study (Saanijoki 2018, Neuropsychopharmacology, n=22 men, doi 10.1038/npp.2017.148) found no overall mu-opioid binding change after 60 min of moderate exercise, though euphoria still went with lower binding.

claim: After a period of wheel running (5 h in the methods; the figure legend says 6 h), mice had higher plasma endocannabinoids, including anandamide, and showed less anxiety and pain. Drug and genetic tests showed that cannabinoid receptors mediate the acute anxiolysis and analgesia: anxiolysis needed CB1 receptors on forebrain GABAergic neurons, and pain relief needed peripheral CB1 and CB2 receptors. Sedation was not affected by blocking either cannabinoid or opioid receptors.
plain: In mice, the calmer, less pain-sensitive behaviour after a long run needed the body's own cannabis-like (cannabinoid) receptors.
source: Fuss J, Steinle J, Bindila L, Auer MK, Kirchherr H, Lutz B, Gass P, 2015, 'A runner's high depends on cannabinoid receptors in mice', PNAS 112:13105-13108
exact_words: We thus demonstrate that the endocannabinoid system is crucial for two main aspects of a runner's high.
who: Mice (wild-type and genetically modified)
limits: These are mice, not people, and euphoria 'cannot be studied in mouse models'. The paper reports the run length inconsistently (5 h vs 6 h).

claim: In a double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled study (N=63), 45 min of moderate-intensity treadmill running increased euphoria and reduced anxiety compared with walking, and raised plasma anandamide and 2-AG. Blocking opioids with naltrexone did not prevent the euphoria, the reduced anxiety or the endocannabinoid rise. The share of people reporting a subjective runner's high was similar under naltrexone and placebo.
plain: Even when a drug blocked people's endorphins, a 45-minute run still made them happier and calmer, so endorphins are probably not the main cause.
source: Siebers M, Biedermann SV, Bindila L, Lutz B, Fuss J, 2021, 'Exercise-induced euphoria and anxiolysis do not depend on endogenous opioids in humans', Psychoneuroendocrinology 126:105173
exact_words: Opioid blockade did not prevent the development of euphoria and reduced anxiety as well as elevation of eCB levels following exercise.
who: Healthy adult participants, N=63, randomized to naltrexone or placebo
limits: It shows opioids are not needed, but it does not prove endocannabinoids cause the high: they were measured in blood and not blocked. It tested a 45-min run, not 2 hours.

claim: Two field studies. In Study 1, 19 trained runners completed a marathon and a duration-matched walk: plasma anandamide (AEA) rose steadily through the marathon and stayed high 45 min after, while walking brought only modest changes; 2-AG rose in the later stages and into early recovery. The marathon was associated with higher euphoria and lower anxiety than walking, while pain increased after 28 km. In Study 2, 36 ultramarathon runners (100, 160 or 230 km) had higher AEA and 2-AG after the race and lower anxiety, but euphoria did not change significantly.
plain: During a marathon, blood levels of the body's 'bliss' chemical (anandamide) kept climbing the longer people ran, and runners felt happier than when walking and a little calmer by the end; after super-long races, no clear rise in happiness was measured and pain was higher.
when: 60+ min (marathon and ultramarathon) and after (45-min break)
source: Siebers M, Huvermann D, Siebers C, Canales-Romero D, et al., Fuss J, 2026, 'Endocannabinoid dynamics across marathon and ultramarathon running: evidence from two field studies', BMC Medicine 24:469
exact_words: AEA increased progressively throughout the marathon and remained elevated after 45 min, whereas walking elicited only modest changes.
who: Trained marathon runners, n=19 (marathon vs walking); ultramarathon runners, n=36
limits: These are blood levels, not brain levels, from small, non-blinded field samples, and they do not show that the chemical causes the feeling. The marathon was always done before the walk, and baseline anxiety was higher on the run day. The discussion calls the marathon anxiety drop 'trend-level'. The ultramarathon had no walking comparison and only before and after samples.

claim: Eight volunteers rowed for 4 hours while blood was sampled at the same time from the radial artery and the internal jugular vein. The brain released BDNF at rest, and this release increased two- to threefold during exercise. At rest and during exercise the brain supplied 70-80% of circulating BDNF, a share that fell after 1 h of recovery. In mice, treadmill exercise raised BDNF mRNA three- to fivefold in the hippocampus and cortex, peaking 2 h after exercise.
plain: During 4 hours of rowing, the brain released 2 to 3 times more BDNF, a 'brain fertilizer' that helps brain cells grow and survive.
source: Rasmussen P, Brassard P, Adser H, Pedersen MV, Leick L, Hart E, Secher NH, Pedersen BK, Pilegaard H, 2009, 'Evidence for a release of brain-derived neurotrophic factor from the brain during exercise', Experimental Physiology 94:1062-1069
exact_words: In humans, a BDNF release from the brain was observed at rest (P < 0.05), and increased two- to threefold during exercise (P < 0.05).
who: Human volunteers, n=8 (4-h rowing); plus mice (treadmill, brain tissue)
limits: With only 8 people, it does not link BDNF to mood, the 'no thinking' state or lasting brain change. The hippocampus and cortex data are from mice.

claim: In a pilot parallel-groups study using MR spectroscopy, 8 experienced yoga practitioners showed a 27% increase in brain GABA (GABA-to-creatine ratio) after a 60-minute yoga session. 11 comparison subjects showed no change after a 60-minute reading session.
plain: After one hour of yoga postures, regular yoga practitioners had about a quarter more GABA, the brain's main 'calm-down' chemical, in the scanned brain area.
source: Streeter CC, Jensen JE, Perlmutter RM, Cabral HJ, Tian H, Terhune DB, Ciraulo DA, Renshaw PF, 2007, 'Yoga Asana sessions increase brain GABA levels: a pilot study', Journal of Alternative and Complementary Medicine 13:419-426
exact_words: These findings demonstrate that in experienced yoga practitioners, brain GABA levels increase after a session of yoga.
who: Yoga practitioners (at least 2 days/week for at least 4 months, 1.5 to 10 years of practice; 6 of 8 had Ashtanga training; 7 of 8 women), n=8, vs non-yoga comparison subjects who read (6 of 11 men), n=11
limits: A tiny pilot with different, non-randomized people in each group (the yoga group was mostly women). Each practitioner did a 60-min asana-and-breathing practice of their own, not a set Ashtanga series. Activity level was not controlled, so other exercise such as walking might raise GABA too, and mood was not measured.

claim: In Fitts and Posner's (1967) model, as Taylor and Ivry (2012) summarise it, skill learning goes through three stages in order. In the cognitive stage the learner sets the task goals and works out which actions to use. In the associative stage the movement is refined. In the autonomous stage practice turns the action into an automatic routine. Across many tasks, learning curves show fast early gains and then slow gains. The core idea is a shift from explicit control at the start to routine control later.
plain: First you think hard about a move, then you polish it, and after lots of practice your body does it on its own.
source: Taylor JA, Ivry RB (2012). The role of strategies in motor learning. Annals of the New York Academy of Sciences 1251:1-12 (summarises Fitts PM, Posner MI 1967, Human Performance, Brooks/Cole)
exact_words: In the Fitts and Posner model, the emphasis is on a shift in control in which initial, explicit control gives way to more routinized forms of control.
who: Classic descriptive model of human skill learning, presented in a narrative review
limits: The stages describe weeks to years of practice, not the first minutes of one class, and the review does not test the model with new data.

claim: People practised memorised finger sequences until they could do them while also counting target letters, with high accuracy on both tasks (the test for automatic). fMRI before and after showed no new brain areas switching on. Instead, activity fell in the cerebellum, pre-supplementary motor area, cingulate, left caudate, premotor, parietal and prefrontal cortex. The authors conclude the same motor network keeps running the movement, but more efficiently.
plain: Once a practised move is automatic, you can do it while thinking of something else, and the same brain areas run it with less activity.
source: Wu T, Kansaku K, Hallett M (2004). How self-initiated memorized movements become automatic: a functional MRI study. Journal of Neurophysiology 91:1690-1698
exact_words: There was less activity in bilateral cerebellum, presupplementary motor area, cingulate cortex, left caudate nucleus, premotor cortex, parietal cortex, and prefrontal cortex during the automatic stage.
who: Healthy adult volunteers learning finger sequences in an fMRI scanner (n not stated in the abstract)
limits: Tests finger tapping in a scanner, not whole-body exercise, and does not show changes within one long session.

claim: Fourteen adults practised an 8-move finger sequence for 15 minutes a day for 4 weeks, with fMRI on days 1, 14 and 28. Activity fell in the associative (rostrodorsal) putamen and rose in the sensorimotor (caudoventral) putamen. Error rate tracked activity in the early-learning areas, and movement speed tracked activity in the later areas, including the sensorimotor putamen and globus pallidus. The authors suggest that learned motor skills end up stored in the sensorimotor part of the basal ganglia.
plain: After weeks of daily practice, activity for a learned move shifts from the thinking part of a deep brain area to its movement part.
source: Lehericy S, Benali H, Van de Moortele PF, Pelegrini-Issac M, Waechter T, Ugurbil K, Doyon J (2005). Distinct basal ganglia territories are engaged in early and advanced motor sequence learning. PNAS 102(35):12566-12571
exact_words: In both putamen, activation decreased with practice in rostrodorsal (associative) regions. In contrast, there was a significant signal increase in more caudoventral (sensorimotor) regions of the putamen.
who: 14 right-handed healthy adults, 15 min of practice a day for 28 days
limits: A finger task in 14 people over a month, not yoga or running, and it does not measure the shift inside one session.

claim: Spinal circuits called central pattern generators (CPGs) can make locomotor rhythms in reduced animal preparations. Whether humans have them is debated. In people with spinal cord injury, spinal cord stimulation or drugs can make the lumbar spinal cord produce rhythmic, step-like muscle patterns without any voluntary control from the brain. In normal walking, CPGs might shape parts of the step cycle and simplify the brain's control of step rate as a feedforward component. This is not yet proven.
plain: Even cut off from the brain, a stimulated human spinal cord can make step-like rhythms; scientists still debate whether, and how much, these circuits help in normal walking.
source: Minassian K, Hofstoetter US, Dzeladini F, Guertin PA, Ijspeert A (2017). The Human Central Pattern Generator for Locomotion: Does It Exist and Contribute to Walking? The Neuroscientist 23(6):649-663
exact_words: In the absence of volitional motor control and step-specific sensory feedback, the human lumbar spinal cord can produce rhythmic muscle activation patterns that closely resemble CPG-induced neural activity of the isolated animal spinal cord.
who: Review of studies in people with spinal cord injury (stimulation or drug-induced rhythms) and of computer models of walking
limits: The rhythm evidence comes from injured, stimulated spinal cords; it does not show that CPGs drive normal running, and it says nothing about yoga.

claim: Human runners phase-lock breathing to stride in several ratios (4:1, 3:1, 2:1, 1:1, 5:2, 3:2), and 2:1 is the most common. In experienced runners, breathing and gait were as tightly coupled as in quadrupeds. In marathon runners, locking happened within the first 4 or 5 strides. Less experienced runners needed longer distances before full coupling. Inexperienced runners showed little or no coupling and irregular breathing. Experienced runners often started at 4:1 and switched to 2:1 as the run went on. Breathing followed the gait, not the other way round.
plain: The most experienced runners' breathing locked onto their steps within a few strides; beginners' breathing mostly stayed irregular.
source: Bramble DM, Carrier DR (1983). Running and breathing in mammals. Science 219(4582):251-256
exact_words: In the most experienced (marathon) runners, phase locking occurred within the first four or five strides of a run.
who: 12 people (11 men, 1 woman, aged 20-45): 6 experienced runners (15-70 miles/week) and 6 with little or no running experience; plus jackrabbits, dogs and horses
limits: Small 1983 sample on runs of up to 1.25 miles with no statistics, and it does not show that coupling saves energy.

claim: Each footstrike pushes air in or out of the lungs ('step-driven flows', peak about 0.97 L/s). Runners naturally preferred coupling patterns that line breath transitions up with the assisting phases of the step and avoid the opposing ones. Breath transitions that started in the preferred phases were about twice as fast as those in the avoided phases. The authors propose that coupling cuts the load on the breathing muscles, the work of breathing and the rate of fatigue.
plain: Every footstep pushes a little air in or out of your lungs, and runners tend to time their breaths to the steps that help, not the ones that fight.
source: Daley MA, Bramble DM, Carrier DR (2013). Impact loading and locomotor-respiratory coordination significantly influence breathing dynamics in running humans. PLoS ONE 8(8):e70752
exact_words: Subjects naturally preferred LRC patterns that minimized antagonistic interactions and aligned ventilatory transitions with assistive phases of the step.
who: 14 adults (9 women, 5 men, mean age 36): 7 recreational runners (20+ miles/week) and 7 fit non-runners, running at a self-chosen speed
limits: The reduction in fatigue and breathing work is a hypothesis; the study did not measure it, and it tested only one speed.

claim: This study tested the constrained-action hypothesis on a balance board (stabilometer). Learners were told to focus either on their own movements (internal focus) or on the effect of the movement (external focus). The external-focus group made generally smaller balance errors and responded at a higher frequency, which the authors read as better blending of voluntary and reflex control. They also had faster probe reaction times, which the authors take as more automatic control. The hypothesis is that focusing on your body interferes with automatic control processes.
plain: On a balance board, people who focused on the effect of the move, not on their own body, balanced better and needed less attention, a sign of more autopilot.
source: Wulf G, McNevin N, Shea CH (2001). The automaticity of complex motor skill learning as a function of attentional focus. Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology A 54(4):1143-1154
exact_words: the external focus participants demonstrated lower probe RTs than did the internal focus participants, indicating a higher degree of automaticity and less conscious interference in the control processes associated with the balance task.
who: Participants learning a balance-board task, told to use an internal or external focus (n and how groups were assigned not stated in the abstract)
limits: A lab balance task, not endurance exercise or yoga, and it does not show effects over long sessions.

claim: Runners ran at a set submaximal treadmill speed while focusing on their running movement, on their breathing, or on a video. Running economy was worse in both internal-focus conditions than in the video condition. Focusing on the running movement also raised vertical oscillation (more bounce), a less efficient style. The authors conclude that consciously attending to the movement pulls runners away from their optimised pattern.
plain: When runners think hard about how they move, they bounce more and use more oxygen at the same speed.
source: Schucker L, Parrington L (2019). Thinking about your running movement makes you less efficient: attentional focus effects on running economy and kinematics. Journal of Sports Sciences 37(6):638-646
exact_words: Therefore, consciously focusing on the running movement moves runners away from their optimised running pattern and leads to detriments in economy.
who: 12 runners on a treadmill at a fixed submaximal speed
limits: A lab treadmill study of 12 runners; not tested in yoga or in sessions of 60 minutes or more.

claim: Active runners ran 24 minutes at a fixed moderate speed in 6-minute blocks. In each block they focused on their movement, their breathing or the feeling of their body, or got no instruction. Focusing on breathing or on movement raised oxygen use (VO2). Focusing on how the body feels gave VO2 similar to the no-instruction control. The authors conclude that internal focus hurts only when it is aimed at highly automated processes such as breathing or movement.
plain: Paying attention to how your body feels did not cost extra energy. Paying attention to your breathing or your running movement did.
source: Schucker L, Knopf C, Strauss B, Hagemann N (2014). An internal focus of attention is not always as bad as its reputation: how specific aspects of internally focused attention do not hinder running efficiency. Journal of Sport & Exercise Psychology 36(3):233-243
exact_words: However, an internal focus on how the body feels during exercise does not disrupt movement efficiency.
who: 32 active runners, one 24-minute treadmill run
limits: 'Breathing focus' here means attending to breathing while running, not yoga's set breath, and the blocks were only 6 minutes each.

claim: Robotic exoskeletons were used to move people's energy-cheapest step frequency higher or lower than their usual one. Walkers changed their step frequency to settle on the new energy optimum within minutes, even when the saving was under 5%. When pushed off the new optimum, they used an updated prediction to get back to it within seconds. The authors conclude that energy cost actively and continuously shapes movement.
plain: Once people had felt a cheaper way to walk, they shifted to it within minutes, even when it saved less than 5% of their energy.
source: Selinger JC, O'Connor SM, Wong JD, Donelan JM (2015). Humans Can Continuously Optimize Energetic Cost during Walking. Current Biology 25(18):2452-2456
exact_words: In response, we found that subjects adapted their step frequency to converge on the new energetic optima within minutes and in response to relatively small savings in cost (<5%).
who: Healthy adults walking in robotic exoskeletons (n not stated in the abstract)
limits: Walking with an imposed energy cost, not running or yoga. Follow-ups from the same lab (J Exp Biol 2019; J Neurophysiol 2019) found that most people do not start optimising on their own: they need experience of the cheaper gaits first, and 20 minutes of varied overground walking did not trigger it.

claim: Ultrasound showed the medial gastrocnemius making force almost isometrically in walking (5 km/h) and running (10 km/h). The Achilles tendon stretched a lot, which let the muscle fascicles work at speeds better suited to producing power. The muscle still did positive work in every condition, and fascicle behaviour changed little across slopes and speeds.
plain: Your Achilles tendon works like a rubber band: it stretches and snaps back, so the calf muscle can hold steady instead of doing all the work.
source: Lichtwark GA, Wilson AM (2006). Interactions between the human gastrocnemius muscle and the Achilles tendon during incline, level and decline locomotion. Journal of Experimental Biology 209:4379-4388
exact_words: Substantial levels of Achilles tendon strain were recorded in both walking and running conditions, which allowed the muscle fascicles to act at speeds more favourable for power production.
who: 6 healthy men walking and running on a treadmill
limits: Only 6 men and short bouts; it does not say how much energy the tendon saves, and Fletcher and MacIntosh (2015, 46 runners) estimated the muscle's energy cost is larger than the tendon's energy return.

claim: This theory paper argues that the human sensorimotor system has (a) high noise and (b) a high learning rate at the synapse. If so, the network needs constant recalibration, and this would explain why expert athletes need a long warm-up before fine-skill performance, beyond warming muscles, tendons and ligaments.
plain: One idea is that the start feels clumsy because your brain's movement settings drift between sessions and need re-tuning each time.
source: Ajemian R, D'Ausilio A, Moorman H, Bizzi E (2010). Why professional athletes need a prolonged period of warm-up and other peculiarities of human motor learning. Journal of Motor Behavior 42(6):381-388
exact_words: They argue that many heuristics of human skill learning, including the need for a prolonged period of warm-up in experts, follow from these assumptions.
who: None (theory and modelling paper, no participants)
limits: A theory with no new human data, framed around fine-skill sports, and not tested in endurance exercise or yoga.

claim: 20 intermediate-to-advanced practitioners followed a 56-minute beginner Ashtanga yoga DVD inside a respiratory chamber; the first 4 minutes were left out of the analysis. Over the 52 minutes analysed they averaged 2.5 METs, 93.2 bpm and 49.4% of age-predicted maximum heart rate, no different from walking at 3.2 km/h. The sun-salutation section lasted 28 minutes, and its last 24 minutes were analysed. It averaged 2.9 METs, 103.5 bpm and 54.8% of predicted max HR, more than walking at 3.2 km/h, and its %HR did not differ from walking at 4.8 km/h. The next 20 minutes of standing poses averaged 2.34 METs and 47.3%, and the last 8 minutes sitting or lying averaged 1.5 METs and 38.7%.
plain: In an hour-long beginner Ashtanga video, the whole class averaged about the effort of a slow walk. The sun salutations were harder, between a slow and a brisk walk, and the rest of the class was easier.
source: Hagins M, Moore W, Rundle A (2007). Does practicing hatha yoga satisfy recommendations for intensity of physical activity which improves and maintains health and cardiovascular fitness? BMC Complementary and Alternative Medicine 7:40
exact_words: Yoga practice incorporating sun salutation postures exceeding the minimum bout of 10 minutes may contribute some portion of sufficiently intense physical activity to improve cardio-respiratory fitness in unfit or sedentary individuals.
who: Intermediate-to-advanced yoga practitioners, n=20 (18 women, 2 men), mean age 31; heart-rate data from 18
limits: This was a beginner-level video lasting 56 minutes, not a 90 to 120 minute Mysore or full primary series practice, and almost all participants were women. Max HR was predicted from age, and the authors warn that %HR may overstate oxygen use during yoga.

claim: Six young adults (18 to 22) with more than 2 years of Surya Namaskar training did four rounds of Surya Namaskar, each round being 12 repetitions back to back (48 in all), in a testing session of about 30 minutes. Their heart rate reached 80% of age-predicted maximum in round 2, 84% in round 3 and 90% in round 4, averaging 80% over the four rounds. Oxygen use averaged 26 ml/kg/min per round, which the author converts to about 230 kcal for a 30-minute session for a 60 kg person.
plain: With each block of 12 sun salutations done back to back, the heart beat faster: about 80%, then 84%, then 90% of its estimated top speed.
source: Mody BS (2011). Acute effects of Surya Namaskar on the cardiovascular & metabolic system. Journal of Bodywork and Movement Therapies 15(3):343-347
exact_words: Participants exercised at 80% of age-predicted maximal heart rate (HRmax) during Round 2, 84% during Round 3, and 90% during Round 4.
who: Healthy Asian Indian men and women aged 18 to 22, trained in Surya Namaskar for more than 2 years, n=6
limits: Only 6 people. A later paper reports that the 48 sun salutations took about 12 minutes, without a teacher, and the sequence was probably the traditional Indian Surya Namaskar, not Ashtanga's Surya A and B. Max HR was estimated from age (220 minus age), the 230 kcal is an extrapolation, and the study does not show what happens later in a long session.

claim: 24 moderately trained adults (12 men, 12 women, mean age 39) did a teacher-led 90-minute vinyasa class twice, with max HR measured on a treadmill test. Mean %HRmax was 58% in the 15-minute warm-up, 72% in 15 minutes of Surya Namaskar, 69% in the following 45 minutes of standing, balancing, sitting and inverted poses with ujjayi, and 55% in the 15-minute cool-down, giving 63% for the whole session. The authors summarise this as 68.8 to 71.7% HRmax for at least 60 minutes.
plain: In a 90-minute flow class the heart was slow in the warm-up, fastest in sun salutations, stayed fairly high for the next 45 minutes, then slowed down at the end.
source: Tsopanidou A, Theodorakou K, Zacharogiannis E (2018). Heart rate response during a Vinyasa yoga session. Science of Gymnastics Journal 10(1):99-110
exact_words: Vinyasa yoga participants in the present study used 68.8%-71.7% of their %HRmax for at least 60 minutes.
who: Moderately trained adults with more than 1 year of yoga, n=24 (12 men, 12 women), mean age 39
limits: This was vinyasa, not Ashtanga. Only heart rate was measured, not oxygen, and in yoga heart rate can run higher than the energy actually used.

claim: A later paper (Tsopanidou et al. 2018) reports that Cowen and Adams measured heart rate in 16 adults (mean age 31.8) over three 80-minute sessions of Astanga, Hatha and Gentle yoga. Mean HR was 95, 80 and 74 bpm, which was 54%, 45% and 42% of HRmax. Astanga gave the highest heart rate of the three. The citing paper classes all three as low-intensity aerobic activity.
plain: In 80-minute classes, Ashtanga made the heart beat faster than hatha or gentle yoga, but by heart rate it was still light exercise.
source: Cowen VS, Adams TB (2007). Heart rate in yoga asana practice: A comparison of styles. Journal of Bodywork and Movement Therapies 11(1):91-95 (doi 10.1016/j.jbmt.2006.08.001). The numbers are as reported in Tsopanidou, Theodorakou and Zacharogiannis (2018), Science of Gymnastics Journal 10(1):99-110
exact_words: Conversely, Cowen and Adams (2007), studying the HR response of sixteen male and female adults (31.8±11.96 years) over three eighty-minute Astanga, Hatha and Gentle yoga sessions respectively, found that the mean HR and %HRmax during sessions was 95±12.84 bpm, 80±9.32 bpm and 74±7.41 bpm, and 54±0.09%, 45±0.06% and 42±0.06% respectively.
who: Male and female adults, n=16, mean age 31.8
limits: I could not open the original paper (Cowen and Adams 2007, J Bodyw Mov Ther 11(1):91-95) and took these numbers from a later paper that cites it. The 'low-intensity' label comes from that citing paper, and a secondary summary says the original authors described a vigorous yoga style as the heart-rate equivalent of moderate exercise. The sample was small, only heart rate was measured, and I found no study measuring oxygen use over a full 90 to 120 minute Ashtanga practice.

claim: 38 adults each did 60 minutes of vinyasa yoga, 60 minutes of brisk walking at their own pace, and 60 minutes of walking at a pace that matched their yoga heart rate. METs were 3.6 for yoga, 4.4 for brisk walking and 4.7 for HR-matched walking. Yoga burned 79.5 kcal less than walking at the same heart rate. Over the first 45 minutes, before the restorative part, yoga energy use did not differ significantly from brisk walking. Yoga met the criteria for moderate-intensity activity.
plain: An hour of flow yoga counts as moderate exercise, but the heart beats faster than the energy you burn would suggest.
source: Sherman SA, Rogers RJ, Davis KK, Minster RL, Creasy SA, Mullarkey NC, O'Dell M, Donahue P, Jakicic JM (2017). Energy Expenditure in Vinyasa Yoga Versus Walking. Journal of Physical Activity and Health 14(8):597-605
exact_words: A similar pattern was observed for metabolic equivalents (HR-Match = 4.7 ± 0.8, SELF = 4.4 ± 0.7, YOGA = 3.6 ± 0.6; P < .001).
who: Adults, n=38 (20 men, 18 women)
limits: This was a 60-minute vinyasa class, not Ashtanga or a 90 to 120 minute session. It measured single sessions only, not fitness changes over time.

claim: A systematic review of 17 studies that measured energy cost by indirect calorimetry (oxygen use) found that yoga practice in the 10 studies of full sessions or Surya Namaskar flows averaged 3.3 ± 1.6 METs (range 1.83 to 7.4), or 2.9 METs without one Surya Namaskar outlier of 7.4 METs. Single asanas averaged 2.2 METs and pranayama 1.3 METs. Yoga is typically light intensity, but a few sequences and poses, including Surya Namaskar, meet the criteria for moderate to vigorous activity.
plain: Most yoga is light exercise. Sun salutations are one of the few parts hard enough to count as moderate or vigorous exercise.
source: Larson-Meyer DE (2016). A Systematic Review of the Energy Cost and Metabolic Intensity of Yoga. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise 48(8):1558-1569
exact_words: However, a few sequences/poses, including Surya Namaskar, meet the criteria for moderate- to vigorous-intensity activity.
who: 17 laboratory studies of yoga sessions, Sun Salutations, single poses and breathing exercises (10 on full sessions or Sun Salutation flows, 8 on single asanas, 5 on pranayama)
limits: The review pooled mostly short measured bouts: Sun Salutation flows, full sessions of various styles, single poses and breathing exercises. It does not report any measurement of a 90 to 120 minute Ashtanga practice, and the abstract does not give per-study styles or sample sizes.

claim: 9 male Army soldiers did 1 hour of yoga training a day, 5 days a week, for 11 months (postures including Surya Namaskar, pranayama and meditation). Tested in the lab during Surya Namaskar after 3, 6 and 11 months of training, their oxygen use was 0.794, 0.738 and 0.560 L/min, and heart rate was 92.1, 97.9 and 87.4 bpm. The drop in oxygen use at 11 months was significant (P < 0.001), and so was the drop in heart rate from 6 to 11 months. Minute ventilation fell from 19.9 to 17.8 L/min, but breathing rate did not drop. The authors conclude that the training conditioned the heart and lungs, and add that the soldiers' regular army training may also have contributed.
plain: After 11 months of practice, 5 days a week, the same sun salutations needed less oxygen. The body seemed to get more efficient at them.
source: Sinha B, Sinha TD (2014). Effect of 11 months of yoga training on cardiorespiratory responses during the actual practice of Surya Namaskar. International Journal of Yoga 7(1):72-75
exact_words: Oxygen consumption and heart rate during actual practice of SN was 0.794 ± 0.252, 0.738 ± 0.229, and 0.560 ± 0.165 L/min and 92.1 ± 11.6, 97.9 ± 7.3 and 87.4 ± 9.2 beats/min respectively at 1(st) , 2(nd) , and 3(rd) phase of yoga training.
who: Healthy male Army soldiers, n=9
limits: Only 9 men, a single group with no control group, and the first test came after 3 months of training, not before it. The soldiers also did regular army physical training, which the authors say may explain part of the change, and getting used to the lab could too. Surya Namaskar was only about 3 min 40 s of each hour, and the practice was not Ashtanga. This was an uncontrolled training study, not purely observational.

claim: 47 premenopausal women aged 35 to 50 were randomised, and 34 completed the study. The yoga group (n=16) did 60-minute Ashtanga sessions twice a week for 8 months: 15 minutes of warm-up, 35 minutes of Ashtanga postures and 10 minutes of cool-down with relaxation, with intensity raised over time. Leg press strength rose 11.4% in the yoga group and fell 6.5% in controls (n=18). Large and small artery compliance did not change, and no other cardiovascular measure (blood pressure, resting heart rate, vascular resistance) changed either.
plain: Women who did Ashtanga twice a week for 8 months got stronger legs, but their arteries and heart measures did not change.
source: Kim S, Bemben MG, Bemben DA (2012). Effects of an 8-month yoga intervention on arterial compliance and muscle strength in premenopausal women. Journal of Sports Science and Medicine 11(2):322-330
exact_words: Eight months of Ashtanga Yoga training was beneficial for improving leg press strength, but not arterial compliance in premenopausal women.
who: Premenopausal women aged 35 to 50: 47 randomised, 34 analysed (16 yoga, 18 control)
limits: Each class had only 35 minutes of Ashtanga postures, twice a week, so this was not a daily 90 to 120 minute practice. 13 of the 47 randomised women dropped out, most of them from the yoga group. Only women were studied, and it shows no heart or artery benefit. Of the other strength tests, only leg press improved.

claim: 17 yoga-naive healthy young adults, lying on their backs, breathed at 6 breaths per minute in different patterns for 2-minute periods. Slow breathing raised cardiac-vagal baroreflex sensitivity, the reflex that steadies heart rate and blood pressure. The biggest gain, and a drop in blood pressure, came with equal inhale and exhale without ujjayi. Ujjayi raised blood oxygen saturation just as much but gave a slightly smaller baroreflex gain and no blood pressure change. With ujjayi on both inhale and exhale, baroreflex sensitivity did not rise significantly. The authors suggest ujjayi's effect depends on higher pressure inside the chest, which takes more effort than plain slow breathing.
plain: In beginners, ujjayi breath raised blood oxygen as much as plain slow breathing, but it boosted the heart's steadying reflex a little less and seems to take more effort.
source: Mason H, Vandoni M, Debarbieri G, Codrons E, Ugargol V, Bernardi L (2013). Cardiovascular and respiratory effect of yogic slow breathing in the yoga beginner: what is the best approach? Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine 2013:743504
exact_words: Ujjayi showed similar increase in oxygen saturation but slightly lesser improvement in baroreflex sensitivity with no change in blood pressure.
who: Yoga-naive healthy young adults, n=17
limits: Participants were beginners who learned ujjayi in about 10 minutes and breathed lying on their backs (supine) for 2-minute bouts, not doing ujjayi while moving through asana. Trained Ashtanga students may respond differently. The extra effort of ujjayi is the authors' explanation, not something they measured directly.

claim: Yoga-naive university students were randomised to a movement-focused or a breath-focused yoga practice. A Florida Tech 'Psychology Science Minute' summary puts it at 40 young adults over 8 weeks. Both groups had lower perceived stress and lower salivary cortisol after the programme, but only the breath-focused group improved sustained attention (response inhibition). Better attention went with lower perceived stress, but not with lower cortisol.
plain: Stress went down in both yoga groups, but attention improved only in the group whose class focused on the breath.
source: Schmalzl L, Powers C, Zanesco AP, Yetz N, Groessl EJ, Saron CD (2018). The effect of movement-focused and breath-focused yoga practice on stress parameters and sustained attention: A randomized controlled pilot study. Consciousness and Cognition 65:109-125
exact_words: While participants of both programs showed a reduction in perceived stress and salivary cortisol, only the breath-focused group showed improvements in sustained attention.
who: Yoga-naive university students (the abstract gives no sample size; a Florida Tech summary says 40 young adults)
limits: A small pilot in beginners, not Ashtanga. It compared two yoga programmes with no non-yoga control group, so the drop in stress cannot be credited to yoga itself. It measured changes over a programme, not what the mind does during one long practice.

claim: 127 Ashtanga practitioners from six US studios were surveyed. Most were women, highly educated and around 40 years old, and they practised on average 4 times a week for over 1.5 hours. They reported experiencing flow during Ashtanga practice and at least moderately endorsed all nine dimensions of flow. Their yoga flow scores were significantly higher than their scores for another physical activity they did now or in the past. More years of Ashtanga, younger age, and intrinsic motivation to accomplish things and to experience sensation all predicted more flow.
plain: Ashtanga students said they get 'in the zone' during practice, more than in another sport they do or did, and more so the more years they have practised.
source: Phillips LL (2005). Examining flow states and motivational perspectives of Ashtanga yoga practitioners. Doctoral dissertation, University of Kentucky (UKnowledge Doctoral Dissertations 336)
exact_words: They reported experiencing flow during ashtanga yoga practice and at least moderately endorsed all nine dimensions of flow state.
who: Ashtanga yoga practitioners from 6 US studios, n=127, mostly women around 40
limits: This is a self-report questionnaire in a doctoral dissertation, not a peer-reviewed paper, with no body or brain measures. Flow was rated as 'at least moderately' endorsed. The study does not say how often flow happens or at which minute of practice it starts.

claim: 10 experienced Ashtanga practitioners (at least 2 years, 3 or more times a week, mean 4.8 years) were compared with 15 matched yoga-naive controls using FDG PET/MR brain imaging. FDG was injected right after practice. After practising the first (primary) series of Ashtanga, the practitioners showed a relative rise in cerebellum glucose metabolism compared with their own rest scan (whole cerebellum +3.2%, peak +4.7%), with no change in absolute metabolism. In the control group, a session of cycling and stretching produced no detectable change. At rest, the practitioners had lower relative metabolism than controls in the medial temporal cortex, striatum and brainstem. In the parahippocampus and brainstem, this was lower the more years they had practised.
plain: Right after the Ashtanga primary series, the cerebellum, the brain's balance-and-movement centre, took a slightly bigger share of the brain's fuel than at rest.
source: van Aalst J, Ceccarini J, Schramm G, Van Weehaeghe D, Rezaei A, Demyttenaere K, Sunaert S, Van Laere K (2020). Long-term Ashtanga yoga practice decreases medial temporal and brainstem glucose metabolism in relation to years of experience. EJNMMI Research 10:50
exact_words: A single yoga practice resulted in significant hypermetabolism in the cerebellum (p < 0.0001).
who: Experienced Ashtanga practitioners, n=10 (8 women), versus 15 matched yoga-naive controls
limits: A very small cross-sectional study that found relative changes only, with no difference in absolute brain metabolism. The yoga session and the cycling and stretching session were done by different people, so the two are not a direct comparison. It cannot show 'no thinking' or that Ashtanga caused the resting differences, and the authors call for a longitudinal study.

claim: WHO 2020 guidelines: all adults should do 150-300 min of moderate-intensity or 75-150 min of vigorous-intensity aerobic activity per week (or an equivalent mix), plus regular muscle-strengthening. Some activity is better than none and more is better for optimal health. Unlike the 2010 version, which required bouts of at least 10 min, bouts of any length now count, because the evidence supports total weekly volume regardless of bout length. Long sessions are therefore not required for health benefit.
plain: The World Health Organization says move 2.5 to 5 hours a week at a moderate pace (or half that if the effort is hard), and short pieces of movement count toward that total too.
source: Bull FC, Al-Ansari SS, Biddle S, et al. (2020). World Health Organization 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour. British Journal of Sports Medicine 54(24):1451-1462.
exact_words: MVPA bouts of any duration now count towards these recommendations, reflecting new evidence to support the value of total physical activity volume, regardless of bout length.
who: Guideline built from systematic reviews of human studies (adults, older adults, children, pregnant and postpartum women, people with chronic conditions or disability)
limits: Gives a weekly total, not an ideal session length, and does not show that a 2-hour session beats several shorter ones.

claim: In a pooled analysis of 661,137 adults followed for a median of 14.2 years, compared with people reporting no leisure activity, mortality risk was 20% lower below the minimum guideline, 31% lower at 1-2x, 37% lower at 2-3x, and reached an upper threshold of benefit at 3-5x the recommended minimum (39% lower). Compared with the minimum, the extra benefit was modest (31% vs 39%). There was no evidence of harm at 10 or more times the minimum.
plain: Moving more is linked to living longer, up to about 3 to 5 times the basic amount. Past that the benefit levels off, and even 10 times the amount showed no sign of harm in this study.
source: Arem H, Moore SC, Patel A, et al. (2015). Leisure time physical activity and mortality: a detailed pooled analysis of the dose-response relationship. JAMA Internal Medicine 175(6):959-967.
exact_words: There was no evidence of harm at 10 or more times the recommended minimum (HR, 0.69 [95% CI, 0.59-0.78]).
who: 661,137 men and women from 6 US and European cohorts, median age 62 (range 21-98), self-reported leisure activity
limits: Self-reported activity and observational design. It shows association, not cause, and does not study yoga or session length.

claim: In human skeletal muscle, training volume may be a critical factor for increasing mitochondrial content, while relative exercise intensity is an important determinant of mitochondrial respiratory function. Changes in content and in function often dissociate.
plain: A lot of total training may build more power plants (mitochondria) in your muscles, while harder effort helps each power plant work better.
source: Granata C, Jamnick NA, Bishop DJ (2018). Training-induced changes in mitochondrial content and respiratory function in human skeletal muscle. Sports Medicine 48(8):1809-1828.
exact_words: Specifically, we report that training volume may be a critical factor affecting changes in mitochondrial content, whereas relative exercise intensity is an important determinant of changes in mitochondrial respiratory function.
who: Review of human endurance-training studies with muscle biopsies (mostly healthy adults)
limits: The authors say 'may be'. Volume means total training, not single-session length, and the review does not show that one long session beats two short ones.

claim: Regular endurance exercise increases the mitochondrial content and respiratory capacity of muscle fibers. As a result, exercise at the same intensity disturbs homeostasis less in trained muscle. Glycogen and blood glucose are used more slowly, fat oxidation is greater, and less lactate is produced. These adaptations play an important role in the large gain in the ability to do prolonged strenuous exercise.
plain: Trained muscles lean more on fat and use up their stored sugar more slowly, so the same work upsets the body less, which helps you keep going for a long time.
source: Holloszy JO, Coyle EF (1984). Adaptations of skeletal muscle to endurance exercise and their metabolic consequences. Journal of Applied Physiology 56(4):831-838.
exact_words: The major metabolic consequences of the adaptations of muscle to endurance exercise are a slower utilization of muscle glycogen and blood glucose, a greater reliance on fat oxidation, and less lactate production during exercise of a given intensity.
who: Narrative review of endurance-training studies on skeletal muscle (trained vs untrained muscle)
limits: An older (1984) narrative review that compares the same absolute intensity. It is about muscle metabolism, not the mental 'autopilot' feeling.

claim: Regular physical activity lowers the risk of insulin resistance, metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes, and insulin sensitivity improves when people meet activity guidelines. Many studies show a dose response, with higher energy expenditure and intensity giving greater benefit, though not all agree. Mechanisms are AMPK-driven GLUT4 translocation during exercise, Akt-driven GLUT4 translocation afterwards, lower intramuscular saturated fat and ceramides, and increased muscle capillarisation as an independent adaptation.
plain: Exercise helps your muscles pull sugar out of the blood, during practice and for a while after. Over time, regular training also grows more tiny blood vessels in muscle, which helps too.
source: Bird SR, Hawley JA (2017). Update on the effects of physical activity on insulin sensitivity in humans. BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine 2(1):e000143.
exact_words: Many studies indicate a dose response, with higher energy expenditures and higher exercise intensities, including high intensity interval training (HIIT), producing greater benefits on whole-body SI, although these findings are not unanimous.
who: Narrative review of human studies (2013-2016 update)
limits: The dose response is not unanimous and weight loss may explain part of the effect. It does not test long single sessions against short ones.

claim: Among 102 healthy seniors grouped by lifelong exercise frequency, 2-3 sessions/week ('casual') did not prevent the age-related stiffening of the left ventricle seen in sedentary people. 4-5 sessions/week ('committed') prevented most of it, and 6-7 sessions/week (Masters athletes) gave the most compliant hearts. Peak oxygen uptake and LV mass rose with dose.
plain: Older people who had exercised 4 to 5 times a week all their adult lives had hearts that stayed more flexible, closer to a young heart. Those who exercised 2 to 3 times a week did no better than people who didn't exercise.
source: Bhella PS, Hastings JL, Fujimoto N, et al., Levine BD (2014). Impact of lifelong exercise 'dose' on left ventricular compliance and distensibility. Journal of the American College of Cardiology 64(12):1257-1266.
exact_words: In contrast, 4 to 5 exercise sessions/week throughout adulthood prevent most of these age-related changes.
who: Healthy seniors, n=102, grouped by self-reported lifelong exercise sessions per week
limits: Cross-sectional with recalled exercise history. It measures how often people trained, not how long each session lasted, and cannot prove cause.

claim: Across 1,237,194 US adults, people who exercised reported 1.49 fewer days of poor mental health per month (43.2% fewer) than matched non-exercisers. The largest associations were for sessions of about 45 min, 3-5 times a week, and more exercise was not always better. The journal's press release adds that small reductions remained above 90 min a day, but more than 3 hours a day was associated with worse mental health than not exercising.
plain: Exercise is linked to fewer days of poor mental health. About 45 minutes, 3 to 5 times a week looked best, and more than 3 hours a day was linked to worse mental health than no exercise at all.
when: whole session (session length and weekly frequency)
source: Chekroud SR, Gueorguieva R, Zheutlin AB, et al., Chekroud AM (2018). Association between physical exercise and mental health in 1.2 million individuals in the USA between 2011 and 2015: a cross-sectional study. Lancet Psychiatry 5(9):739-746.
exact_words: More exercise was not always better.
who: 1,237,194 US adults aged 18+, CDC BRFSS telephone survey (self-report), 2011, 2013 and 2015
limits: Cross-sectional self-report, so very long exercise may be a sign of other problems rather than a cause. The 90-min and 3-h figures come from the press release, not the abstract.

claim: A meta-analysis of 66 studies found that one session of exercise has small benefits for total sleep time, sleep onset latency, sleep efficiency, stage 1 and slow-wave sleep, and a moderate benefit for waking after sleep onset. Regular exercise has small benefits for total sleep time and efficiency, small-to-medium for time to fall asleep, and moderate for sleep quality. Effects varied with exercise type, time of day, duration and adherence, but not with intensity.
plain: People who exercise regularly fall asleep a bit faster and sleep better.
source: Kredlow MA, Capozzoli MC, Hearon BA, Calkins AW, Otto MW (2015). The effects of physical activity on sleep: a meta-analytic review. Journal of Behavioral Medicine 38(3):427-449.
exact_words: Regular exercise has small beneficial effects on total sleep time and sleep efficiency, small-to-medium beneficial effects on sleep onset latency, and moderate beneficial effects on sleep quality.
who: 66 human studies published through May 2013 (mixed ages and fitness levels)
limits: Effects are mostly small. The abstract says duration matters but not that longer sessions are better, and it does not study yoga.

claim: At the 2002 Boston Marathon, 13% of 488 runners who gave a usable finish-line blood sample had hyponatremia (sodium at or below 135 mmol/L) and 0.6% had critical hyponatremia (at or below 120 mmol/L). On multivariate analysis it was associated with weight gain during the race (OR 4.2, 95% CI 2.2-8.2), racing time over 4:00 h versus under 3:30 h (OR 7.4, 95% CI 2.9-23.1) and BMI extremes. On univariate analysis it was also linked to drinking more than 3 litres during the race and drinking at every mile, which suggests drinking more fluid than was lost during long efforts.
plain: In one big marathon, about 1 in 8 runners finished with too little salt in their blood, which can be dangerous. Runners who gained weight during the race (a sign they drank more than they lost) and slower runners were most at risk.
source: Almond CS, Shin AY, Fortescue EB, et al., Greenes DS (2005). Hyponatremia among runners in the Boston Marathon. New England Journal of Medicine 352(15):1550-1556.
exact_words: Considerable weight gain while running, a long racing time, and body-mass-index extremes were associated with hyponatremia
who: Non-elite marathon runners, 766 enrolled, 488 with usable blood samples
limits: Observational study of one race, and only 64% of enrolled runners gave a usable blood sample. It shows links, not cause. It does not cover yoga, where people rarely drink large amounts mid-practice.

claim: Successful training needs overload but must avoid excessive overload combined with inadequate recovery. Functional overreaching leads to better performance after recovery. Without enough recovery, nonfunctional overreaching or overtraining syndrome ('prolonged maladaptation') can develop, with fatigue, falling performance and mood disturbance. None of the markers now used (hormones, performance tests, psychological tests, biochemical and immune markers) meets all the criteria for general acceptance as a diagnostic test.
plain: Hard training helps your performance only when you also recover enough. Too much hard training with too little rest can leave you tired, performing worse and moody.
source: Meeusen R, Duclos M, Foster C, et al. (2013). Prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of the overtraining syndrome: joint consensus statement of the European College of Sport Science and the American College of Sports Medicine. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise 45(1):186-205.
exact_words: Successful training not only must involve overload but also must avoid the combination of excessive overload plus inadequate recovery.
who: Expert consensus based mainly on studies of competitive athletes
limits: Expert consensus with no validated diagnostic test. It does not say how many minutes or sessions is too much.

claim: A meta-analysis of case-control and cohort studies found that athletes had higher odds of atrial fibrillation than non-athlete controls (OR 2.46, 95% CI 1.73-3.51). In meta-regression, mixed sports carried greater risk than endurance sports, and athletes under 55 were at higher risk than athletes 55 and older.
plain: Across many studies, athletes were more likely to have atrial fibrillation, a kind of irregular heartbeat, than non-athletes. The studies did not show how much training it takes to raise the risk.
source: Newman W, Parry-Williams G, Wiles J, et al., O'Driscoll J (2021). Risk of atrial fibrillation in athletes: a systematic review and meta-analysis. British Journal of Sports Medicine 55(21):1233-1238.
exact_words: The risk of developing AF was significantly higher in athletes than in non-athlete controls (OR: 2.46; 95% CI 1.73 to 3.51; p<0.001, Z=4.97).
who: Pooled case-control and cohort studies (1990-2020) of athletes versus physically active or inactive non-athlete controls
limits: Observational, with an odds ratio rather than absolute risk. 'Athletes' means competitive or high-volume sport, not recreational yoga, and exercise dose was not defined (the authors call for dose studies).

claim: Exercising in the heat causes thermoregulatory and other physiological strain that can impair endurance capacity. The most important step to reduce that strain and optimise performance is heat acclimatisation through repeated exercise-heat exposures over 1-2 weeks. Athletes should start training hydrated and minimise dehydration. Unacclimatised participants, mainly in mass-participation events, are at higher risk of heat illness, and organisers should take special care in mass events and on the first hot days of the year.
plain: Exercising in the heat puts more strain on the body and can lower endurance. Experts say the best fix is to train in the heat again and again over 1 to 2 weeks so the body adapts and copes better.
source: Racinais S, Alonso JM, Coutts AJ, et al., Périard JD (2015). Consensus recommendations on training and competing in the heat. British Journal of Sports Medicine 49(18):1164-1173.
exact_words: Exercising in the heat induces thermoregulatory and other physiological strain that can lead to impairments in endurance exercise capacity.
who: Expert consensus focused on athletes training and competing in hot conditions
limits: Focused on athletic performance, and the authors say most heat-stress knowledge comes from military and occupational research. It gives no session-length cut-off and does not study heated yoga rooms.
